reasoning: Decomposed into 104 verifiable statement(s). Completeness check passed. Grouped into 5 reasoning segment(s).

statements: The chief complaint is chronic, progressive right proximal thigh pain in a 20-year-old woman.
The pain has been present for 8 years.
The pain is severe enough to require daily analgesics.
The pain is severe enough to cause sick leave.
The patient’s main concern is persistent unilateral femoral pain.
The pain is worse at night.
The pain worsened further after minor trauma.
There is no evidence of fracture.
The duration of the symptoms is very long.
The pain is localized to the right femur.
MRI demonstrated marked cortical thickening of the right femoral diaphysis.
PET-CT demonstrated marked cortical thickening of the right femoral diaphysis.
MRI and PET-CT showed partial obliteration of the medullary canal.
MRI and PET-CT showed an uneven sclerotic surface.
Bone scan showed increased uptake in most of the right femoral shaft.
The increased uptake on bone scan indicates active bone turnover in that segment.
The patient had a mild leg-length discrepancy.
The patient had prior childhood hip pain on the same side.
Histology showed thickened trabeculae with preserved lamellar structure.
Histology showed accentuated cement lines.
Histology showed no fibrosis.
Histology showed no inflammation.
Histology showed no alcian positivity.
Histology showed no malignancy.
Histology showed no neoplasia.
Bone markers including alkaline phosphatase were normal.
There were no café-au-lait spots.
There were no skin lesions.
The absence of café-au-lait spots or skin lesions argues against syndromic McCune-Albright syndrome.
There was no erythema.
There was no heat.
There was no swelling.
The absence of erythema, heat, or swelling makes chronic osteomyelitis unlikely.
Biopsy showed no inflammation.
There was no malignancy on biopsy.
There was no neoplasia on biopsy.
The absence of malignancy or neoplasia on biopsy argues against osteosarcoma or another primary bone tumor.
The lesion is extensive along most of the femoral shaft.
The lesion is not a small nidus.
The lesion’s extent argues against osteoid osteoma despite nocturnal pain and NSAID responsiveness.
SQSTM1 testing was negative.
The patient is very young.
Negative SQSTM1 testing and young age make Paget disease less likely.
The main candidate differentials are fibrous dysplasia, Paget disease of bone, chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis, and osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma.
Fibrous dysplasia fits several core features best.
Fibrous dysplasia onset can occur in childhood or adolescence.
Fibrous dysplasia can involve a single long bone.
Fibrous dysplasia can cause pain.
Fibrous dysplasia can be associated with mild limb asymmetry or leg-length discrepancy.
Fibrous dysplasia can show expansion and sclerosis of the femur on imaging.
Classic fibrous dysplasia often shows fibro-osseous tissue histologically.
This biopsy showed dense lamellar bone with accentuated cement lines and no fibrosis.
This biopsy pattern is compatible with the sclerotic pagetoid variant of fibrous dysplasia described in monostotic lesions.
The sclerotic pagetoid variant of fibrous dysplasia is described especially in the proximal femur.
The absence of a GNAS1 mutation in blood does not exclude fibrous dysplasia.
GNAS1 mutations in fibrous dysplasia are somatic and mosaic.
GNAS1 mutations in fibrous dysplasia are often absent in peripheral blood.
Paget disease is a consideration because of cortical thickening.
Paget disease is a consideration because of medullary narrowing.
Paget disease is a consideration because of increased uptake on bone scan.
Paget disease is a consideration because of accentuated cement lines on histology.
Paget disease is much less likely in a 20-year-old.
Alkaline phosphatase was normal.
SQSTM1 testing was negative.
The clinical context is childhood onset with a solitary femoral lesion rather than typical adult-onset Paget disease.
Chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis could cause pain.
Chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis could cause sclerosis.
There are no systemic inflammatory signs.
There are no local inflammatory signs.
Biopsy showed no inflammation.
There is no mention of infectious features.
Osteoid osteoma is less likely.
The lesion involves most of the femoral shaft.
The lesion shows diffuse cortical thickening.
The lesion shows medullary obliteration.
The lesion does not show a focal nidus.

The diagnosis that best integrates the age at onset, monostotic unilateral femoral involvement, chronic pain, leg-length discrepancy, imaging pattern, and exclusion of infection and malignancy is monostotic fibrous dysplasia of the femur.
The diagnosis is specifically a sclerotic pagetoid variant.
Monostotic fibrous dysplasia is the high-probability differential diagnosis.
Childhood or adolescent onset supports monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Solitary right femoral involvement supports monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Chronic pain supports monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Mild leg-length discrepancy supports monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Bone scan uptake in the affected shaft supports monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Biopsy excluding malignancy and inflammation supports monostotic fibrous dysplasia.
Blood GNAS1 negativity does not exclude mosaic fibrous dysplasia.
Paget disease of bone is a medium-probability differential diagnosis.
Cortical thickening could resemble Paget disease of bone.
Partial medullary obliteration could resemble Paget disease of bone.
Increased uptake could resemble Paget disease of bone.
Accentuated cement lines could resemble Paget disease of bone.
Age 20 makes Paget disease of bone less likely.
Normal alkaline phosphatase makes Paget disease of bone less likely.
Negative SQSTM1 makes Paget disease of bone less likely.
Chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis can produce painful sclerotic long-bone lesions.
There were no inflammatory signs clinically.
Biopsy showed no inflammation.
Osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma is a low-probability differential diagnosis.
Night pain is suggestive of osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma.
NSAID response is suggestive of osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma.
Diffuse involvement of most of the femoral shaft without a focal nidus argues against osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma.
Biopsy did not show a bone-forming tumor.
The final diagnosis is monostotic fibrous dysplasia of the right femur.
